message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated that there are roughly

\[
10^{43}
\]

different legal positions – this is often called the **Shannon number**.  More recent computational studies that take into account all the rules of chess (including castling rights, en‑passant possibilities, and pawn promotion) suggest that the true count of legal positions is closer to

\[
10^{46}\text{–}10^{47}.
\]

So, while the exact figure is still an open problem, the consensus is that there are on the order of **hundreds of billions of billions of billions** of possible arrangements on a chessboard.
